question: Tell me about a time you had to connect groups that were not communicating. How did you get them working together?

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you had to connect groups that were not communicating.
On my first project, the backend and frontend teams weren't sharing API specs, so my changes kept breaking. I set up a shared doc and weekly 15-min sync after asking my mentor for advice.
We caught issues early and my feature shipped two weeks ahead of schedule. The teams kept the sync going.
How did you handle pushback on the extra meeting?
One engineer said it was overhead, so I kept it to 15 minutes and shared notes; after two weeks they saw value.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you had to connect groups that were not communicating.

Action: created shared doc + 15-min weekly sync after mentor input
Outcome: feature shipped 2 weeks early; sync continued
Quote: "I kept it to 15 minutes and shared notes; after two weeks they saw value"
Follow-up: How did you handle pushback? -> Kept scope small and showed value quickly
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Break down silos. The candidate identified a local communication gap between backend and frontend on their first project and created a lightweight shared doc plus 15-minute sync after checking with their mentor. Quote: "I kept it to 15 minutes and shared notes; after two weeks they saw value." This shows ownership of their immediate work and coachability rather than heroics. The outcome was concrete: the feature shipped two weeks early and the sync stuck. Biggest strength is quick learning from feedback and keeping the fix minimal so it was adopted.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you had to connect groups that were not communicating.
Marketing and product were using different customer data sources, causing conflicting roadmaps. I ran a joint workshop, aligned on a single source of truth, and tracked adoption weekly.
Roadmap conflicts dropped 60 percent and launch delays from misaligned priorities fell from four to one per quarter.
How did you influence without authority?
I started with one-on-ones to surface pain, then invited both leads to co-own the workshop agenda.

senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Break down silos. The candidate bridged marketing and product teams that relied on separate customer data sets, running a workshop and establishing a shared source of truth with weekly tracking. Quote: "I started with one-on-ones to surface pain, then invited both leads to co-own the workshop agenda." This produced measurable cross-team impact: roadmap conflicts fell 60 percent and quarterly launch delays dropped from four to one. Influence without authority is shown through incremental steps rather than mandates. Biggest strength is pairing a concrete process fix with sustained metrics that outlasted the initial effort.

senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Break down silos. Influence stayed within the candidate's own chain rather than building cross-team habits. Biggest gap is reliance on hierarchy instead of creating durable cross-team processes.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you had to connect groups that were not communicating.

Two business units were duplicating platform investments because their roadmaps never intersected. I created a shared platform steering group with rotating leads and tied 20 percent of each unit's OKRs to joint outcomes.
Duplicate spend fell 35 percent over 18 months and one unit's time-to-market improved by nine months.
How did you handle resistance from unit heads?
I framed it as protecting their autonomy on features while reducing shared infra cost, then let them co-define the OKRs.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you had to connect groups that were not communicating.
Role: exec; two business units duplicating platform spend
Action: launched steering group with rotating leads + 20% joint OKRs
Outcome: duplicate spend down 35% in 18 months; one unit time-to-market improved 9 months
Quote: "I framed it as protecting their autonomy on features while reducing shared infra cost, then let them co-define the OKRs"
Follow-up: What was the long-term impact? -> 35% spend reduction; Follow-up: How did you handle resistance? -> Autonomy framing + co-owned OKRs
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Break down silos. The candidate addressed two business units duplicating platform investments by forming a steering group with rotating leads and linking 20 percent of OKRs to joint results. Quote: "I framed it as protecting their autonomy on features while reducing shared infra cost, then let them co-define the OKRs." This produced org-level leverage: 35 percent reduction in duplicate spend over 18 months and a nine-month improvement in one unit's time-to-market. Strategic judgment is visible in preserving unit autonomy while creating shared accountability. Biggest strength is designing a durable governance mechanism that scaled beyond any single project.
